# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# datafusion_openlineage - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/datafusion-openlineage/0.0.7/datafusion_openlineage/

## Expand description

OpenLineage integration for Apache DataFusion.

Instrument a [ SessionState](https://docs.rs/datafusion/54.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion/execution/session_state/struct.SessionState.html)
with

[to emit](https://docs.rs/session/struct.OpenLineage.html#method.builder)

`OpenLineage::builder`[OpenLineage](https://openlineage.io)run events (START / COMPLETE / FAIL) describing each query’s input/output datasets and column-level lineage. Planning-time work (lineage extraction, context, START) runs in a

[; the terminal COMPLETE/FAIL node is installed by a registered](https://docs.rs/rule/struct.OpenLineageQueryPlanner.html)

`QueryPlanner`[that lowers a plan-carried marker — see the](https://docs.rs/rule/struct.LineageExtensionPlanner.html)

`ExtensionPlanner`[module and ADR 0005.](https://docs.rs/rule/index.html)

`rule`The event model, the pluggable [ Transport](https://docs.rs/trait.Transport.html) seam, and the non-blocking

[live in the engine-agnostic](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenLineageClient.html)

`OpenLineageClient`[crate; this crate re-exports them and adds the DataFusion-specific glue. Orchestration metadata (parent run, job ids, custom facets) is injected per query via a](https://docs.rs/openlineage-client/0.0.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/openlineage_client/index.html)

`openlineage_client`[.](https://docs.rs/context/trait.LineageContextProvider.html)

`LineageContextProvider`[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use datafusion::execution::SessionStateBuilder;
use datafusion_openlineage::OpenLineage;
let state = SessionStateBuilder::new_with_default_features().build();
// Reads OPENLINEAGE_URL / _API_KEY / _NAMESPACE / parent-run env vars.
let state = OpenLineage::builder().from_env()?.instrument(state);
```

# sim_lib_pitch_namer_forte - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer-forte/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer_forte/

## Expand description

Forte set-class naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate implements the Forte naming school: it maps a pitch-class set to its
Forte set-class name (such as `4-27` for a dominant seventh) via a lookup
[ FORTE_TABLE](https://docs.rs/constant.FORTE_TABLE.html) of prime-form masks.

[normalizes a](https://docs.rs/fn.lookup_forte_label.html)

`lookup_forte_label`[to prime form before matching, so any transposition or rotation of a set resolves to the same name.](https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-set/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_lib_pitch_set/model/struct.PitchClassMask.html)

`PitchClassMask`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Forte](https://docs.rs/struct.ForteEntry.html)- Entry
- One entry in the Forte table: a prime-form mask and its Forte set-class name.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [FORTE_](https://docs.rs/constant.FORTE_TABLE.html)- TABLE
- The table of known Forte set classes, keyed by prime-form mask.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [lookup_](https://docs.rs/fn.lookup_forte_label.html)- forte_ - label
- Looks up the Forte set-class name for `mask`, normalizing it to prime form first; returns`None`if the set class is not in`FORTE_TABLE`

# bashrs_backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bashrs-backend/0.1.615/bashrs_backend/

## Expand description

POSIX shell backend for xpile (see
`docs/specifications/sub/bashrs-merger.md`).

Implements the [ Backend](https://docs.rs/xpile-backend/0.1.615/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/xpile_backend/trait.Backend.html) trait so

`Target::Shell` has a
registered emitter, and renders **real POSIX shell**for the supported meta-HIR

`Stmt` set. [walks each function body and emits, via the shared [](https://docs.rs/struct.BashrsBackend.html#method.lower)

`BashrsBackend::lower``render_stmt_lines`]
walker: `Stmt::Cmd` → `program arg…`; `Stmt::Pipeline` →
`stage1 | stage2 | …`; `Stmt::ShellAssign` → `NAME=value`; and
`Stmt::ShellLoop` → a multi-line `header; do … done` block whose
body is rendered recursively through the same walker.Args render via [`render_arg`] (`Expr::LitStr` / `QuotedString`
honouring its `QuotingStrategy` / `ShellVar` / `ShellSpecial` /
`CommandSubstitution`). Every emit carries a `#!/bin/sh` shebang
and a `# xpile-contract: C-BASHRS-POSIX-IDEMPOTENCE` citation line
(the same `# xpile-contract: ...` idiom `xpile-rust-codegen` uses,
with `#` for sh’s comment syntax).

A `# (no commands …)` comment is emitted **only** for genuinely
empty input — a module that produces zero renderable statements —
so `xpile transpile empty.sh --target shell` still yields a
well-formed POSIX file. It is a diagnostic for the empty case, not
a stand-in for real emission.

Still future work (out of scope here): a ShellCheck-compatible
verifier, and the structured `Expr::ParamExpansion` /
shell control-flow *parsing* tracked in the bashrs-frontend’s
v0.2.0 fold (param-expansion forms currently survive as verbatim
`Expr::LitStr`).

# xpile_frontend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-frontend/0.1.615/xpile_frontend/

## Expand description

Frontend trait.

Every source language in xpile (Python, C, Ruchy, …) provides
one type implementing [ Frontend](https://docs.rs/trait.Frontend.html). The trait is intentionally
narrow: parse a source file and lower it to canonical meta-HIR.
Everything else — agent loop, oracle, codegen, MCP — is shared.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lowering](https://docs.rs/struct.LoweringProfile.html)- Profile
- PMAT-1034: target capabilities threaded into lowering, extending the
PMAT-1024 `AliasSemantics`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Alias](https://docs.rs/enum.AliasSemantics.html)- Semantics
- PMAT-1024: how the eventual TARGET binds names to objects, threaded into lowering so the frontend’s alias dispositions can be target-aware.
- [Frontend](https://docs.rs/enum.FrontendError.html)- Error

# mado - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mado/0.0.7/mado/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#mado-%E7%AA%93)mado (窓)

macOS active app and window monitoring with browser metadata.

`mado` wraps native macOS APIs through Swift. Use it to query the active
app and focused window, listen to app, window, and bounds changes,
extract browser URL metadata, and scan installed apps from Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

[§](https://docs.rs#query-current-state)Query current state

```
let app = mado::get_active_app()?;
println!("Current app: {}", app);
let window = mado::get_active_window()?;
println!("Window: {}", window);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#monitor-changes)Monitor changes

```
use mado::{WindowListener, WindowMonitor, WindowEvent};
struct MyListener;
impl WindowListener for MyListener {
    fn on_focus_change(&self, event: WindowEvent) {
        match event {
            WindowEvent::AppActivated { app } => {
                println!("App: {}", app);
            }
            WindowEvent::WindowChanged { window } => {
                println!("Window: {}", window);
            }
            WindowEvent::WindowBoundsChanged { window } => {
                println!("Window moved/resized: {:?}", window.bounds);
            }
        }
    }
}
let monitor = WindowMonitor::new(MyListener);
monitor.run()?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#platform-support)Platform Support

- **macOS**: supported
- **Linux**: planned
- **Windows**: planned

[§](https://docs.rs#requirements)Requirements

**macOS:**

- Accessibility permissions required if `track_window_changes`or`track_window_bounds_changes`is enabled

# hamcty - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hamcty/0.3.0/hamcty/

## Expand description

Load and search in a CTY database

licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0,
To view a copy of this license, visit [http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)

Author: Andreas, [df1asc@darc.de](mailto:df1asc@darc.de)

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use hamcty::CountryDatabase;
fn main() {
    // Use crate internal data (maybe not up to date)...
    let cdb = CountryDatabase::new();
    // ...or load data from path (you decide about the version)
    let cdb = CountryDatabase::from_path("test_data/cty.csv").expect("Could not load cty data");
    let call = "DF1ASC";
    assert_eq!(cdb.country(call).unwrap().code, "DL");
    assert_eq!(cdb.prefix(call), Ok("DF".to_string()));
 }
```

- DXCC entity code
- [ITUZone](https://docs.rs/type.ITUZone.html)
- ITU zone number
- [Time](https://docs.rs/type.TimeOffset.html)- Offset
- UTC time offset

# xpile_ffi_manifest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-ffi-manifest/0.1.615/xpile_ffi_manifest/

## Expand description

FFI boundary registry.

In a hybrid transpile (e.g. Python + C extension, Python + CUDA kernel), the agent must know exactly which symbols cross language lines and what their Rust shim signatures should be. This crate is the single source of truth for that mapping within a session.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FfiEmit](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiEmitError.html)- Error
- PMAT-899 (Sprint-2 Tier 2): a reconciled boundary could not be lowered to a
Rust FFI shim because a recovered parameter/return type has no ABI-honest C
mapping (a pointer/string/struct/container the first-cut emitter refuses
rather than mis-marshal). Mirrors `FfiReconcileError`
- [FfiEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiEntry.html)
- [FfiManifest](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiManifest.html)
- [FfiReconcile](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiReconcileError.html)- Error
- PMAT-894 (Sprint-2 Tier 2): a cross-language FFI boundary could not be paired
with a defining module during `FfiManifest::reconcile``C-FFI-CPYTHON-EXT`(the contract’s`manifest_completeness`equation): in a hybrid transpile EVERY boundary that crosses a language line must resolve, or the hybrid build cannot be emitted.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Workspace](https://docs.rs/enum.WorkspaceEmitError.html)- Emit - Error
- PMAT-901 (Sprint-2 Day 2): emitting a buildable hybrid Cargo workspace
failed — either a filesystem error or the shim-emission gap
(`FfiEmitError`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [defining_](https://docs.rs/fn.defining_function.html)- function
- Recover the real defining `Function``FfiManifest::reconcile``to_lang`match.`reconcile`guarantees an entry exists only when the symbol is defined, so a miss here is an internal invariant violation (surfaced as an unsupported boundary by the caller). The defining function for a reconciled boundary: the`Item::Function`named`entry.symbol`in the module whose`source_lang`is`entry.to_lang`. Public so the`--verify`flow (PMAT-902) can read the C callee’s param/return types to build the CPython-side ctypes ABI binding for the differential reference.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_boundary_to_langs.html)- boundary_ - to_ - langs
- PMAT-898 (Sprint-2 Tier 2): resolve each module’s FFI-boundary `to_lang`from the full dispatched module set. A single-file frontend can’t see its siblings, so`depyler-frontend::detect_ffi_boundaries`records a PROVISIONAL`to_lang`(C, the canonical CPython-extension shape) for every relative import. With the whole`Vec<Module>`in hand (the`xpile hybrid`CLI), rewrite each boundary’s`to_lang`to the`source_lang`of whichever sibling module actually DEFINES the symbol. Consequences once`reconcile`runs:
- [retype_](https://docs.rs/fn.retype_float_ffi_sites.html)- float_ - ffi_ - sites
- PMAT-931 (HUNT correctness — the PMAT-930 `c_double`two-arg divergence): after reconciliation, re-type the FFI call sites of every reconciled symbol whose`to_lang`definition returns`Type::F64`so the float-repr path is selected in the calling (Python) module.

# xpile_backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-backend/0.1.615/xpile_backend/

## Expand description

Backend trait — code-lane emission abstraction.

Every target language in xpile (Rust, Ruchy, PTX, WGSL, SPIR-V, Lean)
provides one type implementing [ Backend](https://docs.rs/trait.Backend.html). The trait is intentionally
narrow: take meta-HIR and a config, return an

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)

`Artifact`Sibling of `xpile-frontend::Frontend`. Architectural invariants
codified in `contracts/xpile-backend-trait-v1.yaml`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)
- Emitted artifact — primary source/IR text plus sidecar files plus the structural citation chain to Layer-5 compile contracts.
- [Backend](https://docs.rs/struct.BackendConfig.html)- Config
- Configuration passed to `Backend::lower`
- [Emitted](https://docs.rs/struct.EmittedText.html)- Text
- Plain text emitted by a single `TargetEmitter``Artifact``QuorumStatus`(that’s chosen by the wrapper).
- [Multi](https://docs.rs/struct.MultiEmitterBackend.html)- Emitter - Backend
- Multi-emitter backend wrapper. Composes a general emitter
(mandatory) + an optional specialist under a `QuorumPolicy``Backend``TranspileSession`.
- [ViaEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.ViaEntry.html)
- A single emitter entry from `compile_targets.via`in the YAML schema. Mirrors the structured-record form spec’d in`sub/layer5-multi-emitter-quorum.md`§“Contract YAML schema extension”.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Backend](https://docs.rs/enum.BackendError.html)- Error
- [Diff](https://docs.rs/enum.DiffExecResult.html)- Exec - Result
- Result of a `DiffExec`quorum policy execution. Two PTX (or WGSL/ SPIR-V) programs were run on test inputs; the engine compared their numerical outputs.
- [Emitter](https://docs.rs/enum.EmitterRole.html)- Role
- Role of a backend emitter within a multi-emitter quorum.
- [HwProfile](https://docs.rs/enum.HwProfile.html)
- Hardware profile for targets whose emission depends on hardware
capabilities (PTX `compute_capability`, WGSL feature set, SPIR-V version).
- [Profile](https://docs.rs/enum.Profile.html)
- Lowering profile — the two-mHIR asymmetric decision for Rust↔Ruchy.
- [Quorum](https://docs.rs/enum.QuorumPolicy.html)- Policy
- Policy for combining outputs when both General and Specialist
emitters fire on the same input. Configured per Layer-5 contract
via `compile_targets.quorum_policy`in the YAML.
- [Quorum](https://docs.rs/enum.QuorumStatus.html)- Status
- Status of a multi-emitter quorum vote, attached to an `Artifact`
- [Target](https://docs.rs/enum.Target.html)
- Target language a backend can emit.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Backend](https://docs.rs/trait.Backend.html)
- Code-lane emission trait. See `docs/specifications/sub/backend-trait.md`.
- [Diff](https://docs.rs/trait.DiffExecEngine.html)- Exec - Engine
- PMAT-486 (§30 Track 4): engine that executes two emitted programs on contract-fixture inputs and numerically compares the outputs within a tolerance — the Runtime-stratum half of the §29 quorum. The trait + hook land here (free CI); the real CUDA / Vulkan implementations (PMAT-488 / PMAT-490) run out-of-band on self-hosted GPU runners.
- [Target](https://docs.rs/trait.TargetEmitter.html)- Emitter
- Single-emitter trait — sub-trait of a multi-emitter backend.
One `TargetEmitter``MultiEmitterBackend`

# xpile_meta_hir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-meta-hir/0.1.615/xpile_meta_hir/

## Expand description

Canonical meta-HIR.

Every frontend in xpile lowers its language-specific AST to this
shared, intentionally minimal IR. The federated approach (see
`docs/specifications/xpile-architecture-v1.md`) means we start
lossy and grow as hybrid-transpile cases demand.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.Block.html)
- [FfiBoundary](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiBoundary.html)
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.Function.html)
- [Module](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html)
- [Param](https://docs.rs/struct.Param.html)
- [SortKey](https://docs.rs/struct.SortKey.html)
- PMAT-502z (Tranche 2): a `sorted(xs, key=lambda p: e)`sort key — the lambda’s single parameter name plus its (already-lowered) body. The body is lowered with`param`left unbound (an`Ident`), so it works for bodies that don’t need the param’s precise static type (arithmetic,`len(p)`, most builtins); the backend emits`let <param> = __k.clone();`to bind it by value at runtime. Str-method keys (`p.upper()`) are deferred.
- [TryHandler](https://docs.rs/struct.TryHandler.html)
- PMAT-1059: one `except`clause of a multi-handler statement-form`Stmt::TryCatch``as <name>`message binding, and handler statement block.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [BinOp](https://docs.rs/enum.BinOp.html)
- [Dict](https://docs.rs/enum.DictViewKind.html)- View - Kind
- PMAT-502v (Tranche 2): dict view methods carried by `Expr::DictView`
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)
- [FloatOp](https://docs.rs/enum.FloatOp.html)
- PMAT-477 (R8): float arithmetic operators. Carried by
`Expr::FloatBinOp``Add`/`Sub`/`Mul`/`Div`emit plain infix (`f64`saturates, no`checked_*`);`Div`is IEEE-754 true division. PMAT-502br:`FloorDiv`/`Mod`emit Python-correct*floor*semantics (`(a / b).floor()`and`a - b * (a / b).floor()`), which differ from Rust’s truncating`/`int-div and sign-of-dividend`%`— so they are NOT plain infix.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/enum.Item.html)
- [List](https://docs.rs/enum.ListMutateOp.html)- Mutate - Op
- PMAT-502ap (Tranche 2): no-argument in-place list mutators carried by
`Stmt::ListMutate``Vec`method; all return`None`in Python (so they only appear as expression statements).
- [List](https://docs.rs/enum.ListQueryOp.html)- Query - Op
- PMAT-502u (Tranche 2): list query methods carried by `Expr::ListQuery``Int`;`Index`panics on a missing element (Python`ValueError`).
- [Loop](https://docs.rs/enum.LoopKind.html)- Kind
- POSIX shell loop dialects. PMAT-048 / XPILE-BASHRS-MERGER-001
Layer B. Each variant carries the loop’s control predicate /
item list; the body lives in `Stmt::ShellLoop::body`.
- [NumBuiltin](https://docs.rs/enum.NumBuiltinOp.html)- Op
- PMAT-498 (Tranche 2): scalar numeric builtins carried by
`Expr::NumBuiltin``Abs`takes 1 arg;`Min`/`Max`are variadic (`>= 2`args, PMAT-502cz) and chain`.min`/`.max`over the tail.
- [Pair](https://docs.rs/enum.PairIterKind.html)- Iter - Kind
- PMAT-495 (sprint): the iterator adapter for a `Stmt::ForEachPair`
- [Quoting](https://docs.rs/enum.QuotingStrategy.html)- Strategy
- Per-arg shell quoting choice. Carried by `Expr::QuotedString`so the bashrs-backend renders each arg in the strategy the source indicated. v0.1.0’s bashrs-frontend doesn’t have a real quoting-aware parser yet — it produces`Expr::LitStr`for every arg, and`QuotingStrategy::None`is implicit there. The full strategy set is wired so the v0.2.0 source fold’s real bashrs parser can plug in without IR churn.
- [Radix](https://docs.rs/enum.Radix.html)
- PMAT-502cv: the radix for `hex`/`oct`/`bin`(`Expr::IntRadixStr`).
- [SetOp](https://docs.rs/enum.SetOp.html)
- PMAT-502g (Tranche 2): set-algebra operators carried by `Expr::SetOp``HashSet`method that returns an iterator of borrows, materialized via`.cloned().collect()`into a new owned`HashSet`.
- [SetPred](https://docs.rs/enum.SetPredOp.html)- Op
- PMAT-502ep (Tranche 2): set predicates carried by `Expr::SetPred``bool`. Each maps to a`HashSet`query method; the proper variants additionally require the sets to differ.
- [Source](https://docs.rs/enum.SourceLang.html)- Lang
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)
- [StrMethod](https://docs.rs/enum.StrMethodOp.html)- Op
- PMAT-492 (sprint): no-argument Python string transform methods,
carried by `Expr::StrMethod`
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)
- MVP type lattice. Will grow as frontends demand it. Keep semantically
minimal; map source-language type idiosyncrasies (Python int bigint
promotion, C signed/unsigned, etc.) at the frontend boundary.
PMAT-455 — `Type`is no longer`Copy`because`Type::List(Box<Type>)`is heap-allocated. Callers that previously relied on`*ty`to dereference / copy now use`.clone()`(cheap — most Type values are leaf variants or 1-deep boxes).
- [UnOp](https://docs.rs/enum.UnOp.html)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [collect_](https://docs.rs/fn.collect_block_idents.html)- block_ - idents
- PMAT-736 (HUNT-V11 V11-6): collect every identifier-position name reachable
from `block`into`acc`— both value references (`Expr::Ident`, a`Call`callee) and receiver names (`xs.append(...)`’s`xs`,`d[k] = v`’s`d`, …), plus binding names (a`let`, a loop var). It is the read-only mirror of the`escape_*`walker above: every`escape_name(x)`there becomes`acc.insert(x)`here, so the two stay structurally identical (both are compiler-checked exhaustive over`Stmt`/`Expr`). Used by the frontend’s nested-function lowering to decide whether a nested`def`is self-recursive and whether it captures an enclosing local — over-collection (a binding name, a lambda param) is harmless there, since the caller only intersects the result with the enclosing scope.
- [escape_](https://docs.rs/fn.escape_rust_reserved_idents.html)- rust_ - reserved_ - idents
- PMAT-573: rewrite every identifier in `module`that collides with a Rust keyword to its raw form`r#kw`, so Python locals/params/functions named`type`/`match`/`loop`/… emit valid Rust (and Ruchy). The Rust-family backends call this on a*cloned*module before emission. Struct/enum type names, struct field names, and method names are left unescaped (a keyword-named class/field/method is a separate, rarer fidelity gap).
- [retype_](https://docs.rs/fn.retype_ffi_float_call_sites.html)- ffi_ - float_ - call_ - sites
- Re-type the call sites of `float_ffi`FFI symbols in`module`to F64 so the float-repr path (print`.0`,`let: f64`, float return) is selected. See the PMAT-931 block above. No-op when`float_ffi`is empty.

# xpile_oracle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-oracle/0.1.615/xpile_oracle/

## Expand description

Oracle trait.

An [ Oracle](https://docs.rs/trait.Oracle.html) runs the

*original*source (CPython, gcc-compiled C, the ruchy interpreter) on an input fixture, captures outputs, and lets the agent compare them against transpiled Rust output. This is the semantic gate the agent must pass to exit successfully.

The pattern is borrowed from alchemize: extract reference values
*before* the agent runs, then validate against them.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [CExtension](https://docs.rs/struct.CExtensionOracle.html)- Oracle
- The `cc`-compiled C reference oracle for a single`int(int)`symbol.
- [Captured](https://docs.rs/struct.CapturedOutputs.html)- Outputs
- [Ctypes](https://docs.rs/struct.CtypesBinding.html)- Binding
- One boundary symbol’s `ctypes`ABI for the CPython hybrid reference.`argtypes`/`restype`are bare`ctypes`type names (e.g.`"c_int"`,`"c_double"`);`restype == None`binds a`void`callee (`restype = None`).
- [Fixture](https://docs.rs/struct.Fixture.html)
- [Python](https://docs.rs/struct.PythonOracle.html)- Oracle
- The CPython reference oracle. Captures the stdout of running a Python module’s
`main()`under the system`python3`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_cpython_hybrid_ref.html)- cpython_ - hybrid_ - ref
- Capture the CPython reference for a hybrid Python+C module: `cc`-compile`c_sources`into a shared object, bind each`CtypesBinding`symbol via`ctypes`, strip the C-extension relative import from`py_source`, and run its`main()`under`python3`, returning stdout (trailing newline trimmed). Requires`cc`+`python3`; callers should graceful-skip when either is absent (mirror`PythonOracle::available``CExtensionOracle::available`
- [diff_](https://docs.rs/fn.diff_stdout.html)- stdout
- Compare two captured stdout strings (CPython reference vs transpiled-Rust).
Returns `ComparisonResult::Match``Divergence`pinning the first differing line for a readable failure message.

# yew 0.23.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/yew/0.23.0

## About

**Yew** is a modern Rust framework for creating multi-threaded, front-end web apps with WebAssembly.

- Features a macro for declaring interactive HTML with Rust expressions. Developers who have experience using JSX in React should feel quite at home when using Yew.
- Achieves high performance by minimizing DOM API calls for each page render and by making it easy to offload processing to background web workers.
- Supports JavaScript interoperability, allowing developers to leverage NPM packages and integrate with existing JavaScript applications.

Yew is named after a type of evergreen tree, and is pronounced /juː/. [Entry with audio on Cambridge Dictionary](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/yew).

*Note: Yew is not 1.0 yet. Be prepared to do major refactoring due to breaking API changes.*

## Contributing

Yew is a community-driven effort and we welcome all kinds of contributions, big or small, from developers of all backgrounds. We want the Yew community to be a fun and friendly place, so please review our [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/yewstack/yew/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) to learn what behavior will not be tolerated.

#### 🤠 New to Yew?

Start learning about the framework by helping us improve our [documentation](https://github.com/yewstack/yew/tree/master/website/docs). Pull requests which improve test coverage are also very welcome.

#### 😎 Looking for inspiration?

Check out the community curated list of awesome things related to Yew / WebAssembly at [jetli/awesome-yew](https://github.com/jetli/awesome-yew).

#### 🤔 Confused about something?

Feel free to drop into our [Discord chatroom](https://discord.gg/VQck8X4) or open a [new "Question" issue](https://github.com/yewstack/yew/issues/new/choose) to get help from contributors. Often questions lead to improvements to the ergonomics of the framework, better documentation and even new features!

#### 🙂 Ready to dive into the code?

After reviewing the [Contribution Guide](https://github.com/yewstack/yew/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md), check out the ["Good First Issues"](https://github.com/yewstack/yew/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22) (they are eager for attention!). Once you find one that interests you, feel free to assign yourself to an issue and don't hesitate to reach out for guidance, the issues vary in complexity.

#### 😱 Found a bug?

Please [report all bugs!](https://github.com/yewstack/yew/issues/new/choose) We are happy to help support developers fix the bugs they find if they are interested and have the time.

## Contributors

### Code Contributors

This project exists thanks to all the people who contribute.

### Financial Contributors

Become a financial contributor and help us sustain our community. [[Contribute](https://opencollective.com/yew/contribute)]

#### Individuals

#### Organizations

Support this project with your organization. Your logo will show up here with a link to your website. [[Contribute](https://opencollective.com/yew/contribute)]

# yew - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/yew/0.23.0/target-redirect/yew/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#yew-framework---api-documentation)Yew Framework - API Documentation

Yew is a modern Rust framework for creating multi-threaded front-end web apps using WebAssembly

- Features a macro for declaring interactive HTML with Rust expressions. Developers who have experience using JSX in React should feel quite at home when using Yew.
- Achieves high performance by minimizing DOM API calls for each page render and by making it easy to offload processing to background web workers.
- Supports JavaScript interoperability, allowing developers to leverage NPM packages and integrate with existing JavaScript applications.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-targets-client-side-rendering)Supported Targets (Client-Side Rendering)

- `wasm32-unknown-unknown`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Server-Side Rendering should work on all targets when feature `ssr` is enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-features)Supported Features:

- `csr`: Enables Client-side Rendering support and- `Renderer`
- `ssr`: Enables Server-side Rendering support and- `ServerRenderer`
- `hydration`: Enables Hydration support.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yew::prelude::*;
enum Msg {
    AddOne,
}
struct App {
    value: i64,
}
impl Component for App {
    type Message = Msg;
    type Properties = ();
    fn create(ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Self {
        Self { value: 0 }
    }
    fn update(&mut self, _ctx: &Context<Self>, msg: Self::Message) -> bool {
        match msg {
            Msg::AddOne => {
                self.value += 1;
                true
            }
        }
    }
    fn view(&self, ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Html {
        html! {
            <div>
                <button onclick={ctx.link().callback(|_| Msg::AddOne)}>{ "+1" }</button>
                <p>{ self.value }</p>
            </div>
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    yew::Renderer::<App>::new().render();
}
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use self::`- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)::*;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [callback](https://docs.rs/callback/index.html)
- This module contains data types for interacting with `Scope`s.
- [context](https://docs.rs/context/index.html)
- This module defines the `ContextProvider`component.
- [events](https://docs.rs/events/index.html)
- The module that contains all events available in the framework.
- [functional](https://docs.rs/functional/index.html)
- Function components are a simplified version of normal components.
They consist of a single function annotated with the attribute `#[component]`that receives props and determines what should be rendered by returning`Html`
- [html](https://docs.rs/html/index.html)
- The main html module which defines components, listeners, and class helpers.
- [macros](https://docs.rs/macros/index.html)
- This module contains macros which implements html! macro and JSX-like templates
- [platform](https://docs.rs/platform/index.html)
- Yew’s compatibility between JavaScript Runtime and Native Runtimes.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- The Yew Prelude
- [scheduler](https://docs.rs/scheduler/index.html)
- This module contains a scheduler.
- [suspense](https://docs.rs/suspense/index.html)
- This module provides suspense support.
- [tests](https://docs.rs/tests/index.html)- `csr`and (- `test`)
- Internal module for unit tests
- [utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)
- This module contains useful utilities to get information about the current document.
- [virtual_](https://docs.rs/virtual_dom/index.html)- dom
- This module contains Yew’s implementation of a reactive virtual DOM.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [classes](https://docs.rs/macro.classes.html)
- This macro provides a convenient way to create `Classes`
- [html](https://docs.rs/macro.html.html)
- This macro implements JSX-like templates.
- [html_](https://docs.rs/macro.html_nested.html)- nested
- This macro is similar to `html!``Html`
- [props](https://docs.rs/macro.props.html)

# yew - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew/0.23.0/yew/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#yew-framework---api-documentation)Yew Framework - API Documentation

Yew is a modern Rust framework for creating multi-threaded front-end web apps using WebAssembly

- Features a macro for declaring interactive HTML with Rust expressions. Developers who have experience using JSX in React should feel quite at home when using Yew.
- Achieves high performance by minimizing DOM API calls for each page render and by making it easy to offload processing to background web workers.
- Supports JavaScript interoperability, allowing developers to leverage NPM packages and integrate with existing JavaScript applications.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-targets-client-side-rendering)Supported Targets (Client-Side Rendering)

- `wasm32-unknown-unknown`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Server-Side Rendering should work on all targets when feature `ssr` is enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-features)Supported Features:

- `csr`: Enables Client-side Rendering support and- `Renderer`
- `ssr`: Enables Server-side Rendering support and- `ServerRenderer`
- `hydration`: Enables Hydration support.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yew::prelude::*;
enum Msg {
    AddOne,
}
struct App {
    value: i64,
}
impl Component for App {
    type Message = Msg;
    type Properties = ();
    fn create(ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Self {
        Self { value: 0 }
    }
    fn update(&mut self, _ctx: &Context<Self>, msg: Self::Message) -> bool {
        match msg {
            Msg::AddOne => {
                self.value += 1;
                true
            }
        }
    }
    fn view(&self, ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Html {
        html! {
            <div>
                <button onclick={ctx.link().callback(|_| Msg::AddOne)}>{ "+1" }</button>
                <p>{ self.value }</p>
            </div>
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    yew::Renderer::<App>::new().render();
}
```

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [callback](https://docs.rs/callback/index.html)
- This module contains data types for interacting with `Scope`s.
- [context](https://docs.rs/context/index.html)
- This module defines the `ContextProvider`component.
- [events](https://docs.rs/events/index.html)
- The module that contains all events available in the framework.
- [functional](https://docs.rs/functional/index.html)
- Function components are a simplified version of normal components.
They consist of a single function annotated with the attribute `#[component]`that receives props and determines what should be rendered by returning`Html`
- [html](https://docs.rs/html/index.html)
- The main html module which defines components, listeners, and class helpers.
- [macros](https://docs.rs/macros/index.html)
- This module contains macros which implements html! macro and JSX-like templates
- [platform](https://docs.rs/platform/index.html)
- Yew’s compatibility between JavaScript Runtime and Native Runtimes.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- The Yew Prelude
- [scheduler](https://docs.rs/scheduler/index.html)
- This module contains a scheduler.
- [suspense](https://docs.rs/suspense/index.html)
- This module provides suspense support.
- [tests](https://docs.rs/tests/index.html)- `csr`and (- `test`)
- Internal module for unit tests
- [utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)
- This module contains useful utilities to get information about the current document.
- [virtual_](https://docs.rs/virtual_dom/index.html)- dom
- This module contains Yew’s implementation of a reactive virtual DOM.

[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! # Yew Framework - API Documentation
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! Yew is a modern Rust framework for creating multi-threaded front-end web apps using WebAssembly
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! - Features a macro for declaring interactive HTML with Rust expressions. Developers who have
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!   experience using JSX in React should feel quite at home when using Yew.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! - Achieves high performance by minimizing DOM API calls for each page render and by making it
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!   easy to offload processing to background web workers.
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! - Supports JavaScript interoperability, allowing developers to leverage NPM packages and
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!   integrate with existing JavaScript applications.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! ### Supported Targets (Client-Side Rendering)
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! - `wasm32-unknown-unknown`
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! ### Note
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! Server-Side Rendering should work on all targets when feature `ssr` is enabled.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! ### Supported Features:
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! - `csr`: Enables Client-side Rendering support and [`Renderer`]. Only enable this feature if you
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!   are making a Yew application (not a library).
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! - `ssr`: Enables Server-side Rendering support and [`ServerRenderer`].
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! - `hydration`: Enables Hydration support.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! ## Example
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! ```rust,no_run
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! use yew::prelude::*;
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! enum Msg {
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!     AddOne,
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! }
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! struct App {
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!     value: i64,
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! }
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! impl Component for App {
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!     type Message = Msg;
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!     type Properties = ();
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!     fn create(ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Self {
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!         Self { value: 0 }
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!     }
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!     fn update(&mut self, _ctx: &Context<Self>, msg: Self::Message) -> bool {
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!         match msg {
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!             Msg::AddOne => {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!                 self.value += 1;
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!                 true
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!             }
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!         }
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!     }
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!     fn view(&self, ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Html {
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!         html! {
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!             <div>
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!                 <button onclick={ctx.link().callback(|_| Msg::AddOne)}>{ "+1" }</button>
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!                 <p>{ self.value }</p>
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!             </div>
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!         }
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!     }
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! }
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! fn main() {
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!     yew::Renderer::<App>::new().render();
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! }
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! ```
[74](https://docs.rs#74)
[75](https://docs.rs#75)#![deny(
[76](https://docs.rs#76)    missing_docs,
[77](https://docs.rs#77)    missing_debug_implementations,
[78](https://docs.rs#78)    bare_trait_objects,
[79](https://docs.rs#79)    anonymous_parameters,
[80](https://docs.rs#80)    elided_lifetimes_in_paths
[81](https://docs.rs#81))]
[82](https://docs.rs#82)#![allow(macro_expanded_macro_exports_accessed_by_absolute_paths)]
[83](https://docs.rs#83)#![recursion_limit = "512"]
[84](https://docs.rs#84)extern crate self as yew;
[85](https://docs.rs#85)
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// This macro provides a convenient way to create [`Classes`].
[87](https://docs.rs#87)///
[88](https://docs.rs#88)/// The macro takes a list of items similar to the [`vec!`] macro and returns a [`Classes`]
[89](https://docs.rs#89)/// instance. Each item can be of any type that implements `Into<Classes>` (See the
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// implementations on [`Classes`] to learn what types can be used).
[91](https://docs.rs#91)///
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// # Example
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// ```
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// # use yew::prelude::*;
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// # fn test() {
[97](https://docs.rs#97)/// let conditional_class = Some("my-other-class");
[98](https://docs.rs#98)/// let vec_of_classes = vec![
[99](https://docs.rs#99)///     "one-bean",
[100](https://docs.rs#100)///     "two-beans",
[101](https://docs.rs#101)///     "three-beans",
[102](https://docs.rs#102)///     "a-very-small-casserole",
[103](https://docs.rs#103)/// ];
[104](https://docs.rs#104)///
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// html! {
[106](https://docs.rs#106)///     <div class={classes!("my-container-class", conditional_class, vec_of_classes)}>
[107](https://docs.rs#107)///         // ...
[108](https://docs.rs#108)///     </div>
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// };
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// # }
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// ```
[112](https://docs.rs#112)pub use yew_macro::classes;
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// This macro implements JSX-like templates.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)///
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// This macro always returns [`Html`].
[116](https://docs.rs#116)/// If you need to preserve the type of a component, use the [`html_nested!`] macro instead.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)///
[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// More information about using the `html!` macro can be found in the [Yew Docs]
[119](https://docs.rs#119)///
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// [`Html`]: ./html/type.Html.html
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// [`html_nested!`]: ./macro.html_nested.html
[122](https://docs.rs#122)/// [Yew Docs]: https://yew.rs/docs/next/concepts/html
[123](https://docs.rs#123)pub use yew_macro::html;
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// This macro is similar to [`html!`], but preserves the component type instead
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// of wrapping it in [`Html`].
[126](https://docs.rs#126)///
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// That macro is useful when, for example, in a typical implementation of a list
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// component (let's assume it's called `List`).
[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// In a typical implementation you might find two component types -- `List` and `ListItem`.
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// Only `ListItem` components are allowed to be children of List`.
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// You can find an example implementation of this in the [`nested_list`] example.
[133](https://docs.rs#133)/// That example shows, how to create static lists with their children.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)///
[135](https://docs.rs#135)/// ```
[136](https://docs.rs#136)/// # use yew::prelude::*;
[137](https://docs.rs#137)/// use yew::html::ChildrenRenderer;
[138](https://docs.rs#138)/// use yew::virtual_dom::VChild;
[139](https://docs.rs#139)///
[140](https://docs.rs#140)/// #[derive(Clone, Properties, PartialEq)]
[141](https://docs.rs#141)/// struct ListProps {
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///     children: ChildrenRenderer<ListItem>,
[143](https://docs.rs#143)/// }
[144](https://docs.rs#144)///
[145](https://docs.rs#145)/// struct List;
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// impl Component for List {
[147](https://docs.rs#147)/// #   type Message = ();
[148](https://docs.rs#148)///     type Properties = ListProps;
[149](https://docs.rs#149)///     // ...
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// #   fn create(ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Self { Self }
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// #   fn view(&self, ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Html { unimplemented!() }
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)///
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// #[derive(Clone, PartialEq)]
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// struct ListItem;
[156](https://docs.rs#156)/// impl Component for ListItem {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// #   type Message = ();
[158](https://docs.rs#158)/// #   type Properties = ();
[159](https://docs.rs#159)///     // ...
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// #   fn create(ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Self { Self }
[161](https://docs.rs#161)/// #   fn view(&self, ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Html { unimplemented!() }
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// }
[163](https://docs.rs#163)///
[164](https://docs.rs#164)/// // Required for ChildrenRenderer
[165](https://docs.rs#165)/// impl From<VChild<ListItem>> for ListItem {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)///     fn from(child: VChild<ListItem>) -> Self {
[167](https://docs.rs#167)///         Self
[168](https://docs.rs#168)///     }
[169](https://docs.rs#169)/// }
[170](https://docs.rs#170)///
[171](https://docs.rs#171)/// impl Into<Html> for ListItem {
[172](https://docs.rs#172)///     fn into(self) -> Html {
[173](https://docs.rs#173)///         html! { <self /> }
[174](https://docs.rs#174)///     }
[175](https://docs.rs#175)/// }
[176](https://docs.rs#176)/// // You can use `List` with nested `ListItem` components.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// // Using any other kind of element would result in a compile error.
[178](https://docs.rs#178)/// # fn test() -> Html {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)/// html! {
[180](https://docs.rs#180)///   <List>
[181](https://docs.rs#181)///     <ListItem/>
[182](https://docs.rs#182)///     <ListItem/>
[183](https://docs.rs#183)///     <ListItem/>
[184](https://docs.rs#184)///   </List>
[185](https://docs.rs#185)/// }
[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// # }
[187](https://docs.rs#187)/// # fn test_iter() -> Html {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// # let some_iter = (0..10);
[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// // In many cases you might want to create the content dynamically.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)/// // To do this, you can use the following code:
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// html! {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)///   <List>
[193](https://docs.rs#193)///     { for some_iter.map(|_| html_nested!{ <ListItem/> }) }
[194](https://docs.rs#194)///   </List>
[195](https://docs.rs#195)/// }
[196](https://docs.rs#196)/// # }
[197](https://docs.rs#197)/// ```
[198](https://docs.rs#198)///
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// If you used the [`html!`] macro instead of `html_nested!`, the code would
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// not compile because we explicitly indicated to the compiler that `List`
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// can only contain elements of type `ListItem` using [`ChildrenRenderer<ListItem>`],
[202](https://docs.rs#202)/// while [`html!`] creates items of type [`Html`].
[203](https://docs.rs#203)///
[204](https://docs.rs#204)///
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// [`html!`]: ./macro.html.html
[206](https://docs.rs#206)/// [`Html`]: ./html/type.Html.html
[207](https://docs.rs#207)/// [`nested_list`]: https://github.com/yewstack/yew/tree/master/examples/nested_list
[208](https://docs.rs#208)/// [`ChildrenRenderer<ListItem>`]: ./html/struct.ChildrenRenderer.html
[209](https://docs.rs#209)pub use yew_macro::html_nested;
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// Build [`Properties`] outside of the [`html!`] macro.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// It's already possible to create properties like normal Rust structs
[213](https://docs.rs#213)/// but if there are lots of optional props the end result is often needlessly verbose.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// This macro allows you to build properties the same way the [`html!`] macro does.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)///
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// The macro doesn't support special props like `ref` and `key`, they need to be set in the
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// [`html!`] macro.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// You can read more about `Properties` in the [Yew Docs].
[220](https://docs.rs#220)///
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// # Example
[222](https://docs.rs#222)///
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// ```
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// # use yew::prelude::*;
[225](https://docs.rs#225)/// use std::borrow::Cow;
[226](https://docs.rs#226)///
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// #[derive(Clone, Properties, PartialEq)]
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// struct Props {
[229](https://docs.rs#229)///     #[prop_or_default]
[230](https://docs.rs#230)///     id: usize,
[231](https://docs.rs#231)///     name: Cow<'static, str>,
[232](https://docs.rs#232)/// }
[233](https://docs.rs#233)///
[234](https://docs.rs#234)/// struct MyComponent(Props);
[235](https://docs.rs#235)/// impl Component for MyComponent {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)/// #   type Message = ();
[237](https://docs.rs#237)///     type Properties = Props;
[238](https://docs.rs#238)///     // ...
[239](https://docs.rs#239)/// #   fn create(ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Self { unimplemented!() }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)/// #   fn view(&self, ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Html { unimplemented!() }
[241](https://docs.rs#241)/// }
[242](https://docs.rs#242)///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)/// # fn foo() -> Html {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)/// // You can build props directly ...
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// let props = yew::props!(Props {
[246](https://docs.rs#246)///     name: Cow::from("Minka")
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// });
[248](https://docs.rs#248)/// # assert_eq!(props.name, "Minka");
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// // ... or build the associated properties of a component
[250](https://docs.rs#250)/// let props = yew::props!(MyComponent::Properties {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)///     id: 2,
[252](https://docs.rs#252)///     name: Cow::from("Lemmy")
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// });
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// # assert_eq!(props.id, 2);
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// // Use the Rust-like struct update syntax to create a component with the props.
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// html! {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)///     <MyComponent key=1 ..props />
[259](https://docs.rs#259)/// }
[260](https://docs.rs#260)/// # }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)/// ```
[262](https://docs.rs#262)///
[263](https://docs.rs#263)/// [`html!`]: ./macro.html.html
[264](https://docs.rs#264)/// [`Properties`]: ./html/trait.Properties.html
[265](https://docs.rs#265)/// [Yew Docs]: https://yew.rs/concepts/components/properties
[266](https://docs.rs#266)pub use yew_macro::props;
[267](https://docs.rs#267)

# yew::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew/0.23.0/yew/prelude/index.html

## Expand description

The Yew Prelude

The purpose of this module is to alleviate imports of many common types:

`use yew::prelude::*;`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::callback::`- [Callback](https://docs.rs/callback/struct.Callback.html);

- `pub use crate::callback::`- [CallbackRefMut](https://docs.rs/callback/struct.CallbackRefMut.html);
- `pub use crate::context::`- [ContextHandle](https://docs.rs/context/struct.ContextHandle.html);
- `pub use crate::context::`- [ContextProvider](https://docs.rs/context/struct.ContextProvider.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [create_portal](https://docs.rs/html/fn.create_portal.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [BaseComponent](https://docs.rs/html/trait.BaseComponent.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [Children](https://docs.rs/html/type.Children.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [ChildrenWithProps](https://docs.rs/html/type.ChildrenWithProps.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [Classes](https://docs.rs/html/struct.Classes.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [Component](https://docs.rs/html/trait.Component.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [Context](https://docs.rs/html/struct.Context.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [Html](https://docs.rs/html/type.Html.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [HtmlResult](https://docs.rs/html/type.HtmlResult.html);
- `pub use crate::html::`- [NodeRef](https://docs.rs/html/struct.NodeRef.html);

- `pub use crate::virtual_dom::`- [AttrValue](https://docs.rs/virtual_dom/type.AttrValue.html);
- `pub use crate::`- [events](https://docs.rs/events/index.html)::*;
- `pub use crate::`- [functional](https://docs.rs/functional/index.html)::*;

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [classes](https://docs.rs/macro.classes.html)
- This macro provides a convenient way to create `Classes`
- [html](https://docs.rs/macro.html.html)
- This macro implements JSX-like templates.

# yew::functional - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew/0.23.0/yew/functional/index.html

## Expand description

Function components are a simplified version of normal components.
They consist of a single function annotated with the attribute `#[component]`
that receives props and determines what should be rendered by returning [ Html](https://docs.rs/html/type.Html.html).

Functions with the attribute have to return `Html` and may take a single parameter for the type
of props the component should accept. The parameter type needs to be a reference to a
`Properties` type (ex. `props: &MyProps`). If the function doesn’t have any parameters the
resulting component doesn’t accept any props.

Just mark the component with the attribute. The component will be named after the function.

```
#[component]
fn HelloWorld() -> Html {
    html! { "Hello world" }
}
```
More details about function components and Hooks can be found on [Yew Docs](https://yew.rs/docs/next/concepts/function-components/introduction)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [use_](https://docs.rs/macro.use_prepared_state.html)- prepared_ - state
- Use a state prepared on the server side and its value is sent to the client side during hydration.
- [use_](https://docs.rs/macro.use_transitive_state.html)- transitive_ - state
- Use a state created as an artifact of the server-side rendering.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A hook context to be passed to hooks.
- [UseForce](https://docs.rs/struct.UseForceUpdateHandle.html)- Update - Handle
- A handle which can be used to force a re-render of the associated function component.

# yew::platform - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew/0.23.0/yew/platform/index.html

## Expand description

Yew’s compatibility between JavaScript Runtime and Native Runtimes.

This module is also published under the name [tokise](https://docs.rs/tokise/0.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokise/index.html) on crates.io.

[§](https://docs.rs#rationale)Rationale

When designing components and libraries that works on both WebAssembly targets backed by JavaScript Runtime and non-WebAssembly targets with Native Runtimes. Developers usually face challenges that requires applying multiple feature flags throughout their application:

- Select I/O and timers that works with the target runtime.
- Native Runtimes usually require `Send`futures and WebAssembly types are usually`!Send`.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

To alleviate these issues, Yew implements a single-threaded runtime that executes `?Send`
(`Send` or `!Send`) futures.

On platforms with multi-threading support, Yew spawns multiple independent runtimes
proportional to the CPU core number. When tasks are spawned with a runtime handle, it will
randomly select a worker thread from the internal pool. All tasks spawned with `spawn_local`
will run on the same thread as the thread the task was running. When the runtime runs in a
WebAssembly target, all tasks will be scheduled on the main thread.

This runtime is designed in favour of IO-bounded workload with similar runtime cost. When running I/O workloads, it would produce a slightly better performance as tasks are never moved to another thread. However, If a worker thread is busy, other threads will not be able to steal tasks scheduled on the busy thread. When you have a CPU-bounded task where CPU time is significantly more expensive, it should be spawned with a dedicated thread (or Web Worker) and communicates with the application using channels.

Yew platform provides the following components:

- A Task Scheduler that is capable of running non-Send tasks.
- A Timer that is compatible with the scheduler backend.
- Task Synchronisation Mechanisms.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-backend)Runtime Backend

The Yew runtime is implemented with different runtimes depending on the target platform and can use all features (timers / IO / task synchronisation) from the selected native runtime:

- `wasm-bindgen-futures`(WebAssembly targets)
- `tokio`(non-WebAssembly targets)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [fmt](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html)
- Asynchronous utilities to work with `String`s.
- [pinned](https://docs.rs/pinned/index.html)
- Task synchronisation primitives for pinned tasks.
- [time](https://docs.rs/time/index.html)
- Utilities for bridging time and tasks.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.LocalHandle.html)- Handle
- A Local Runtime Handle.
- [Runtime](https://docs.rs/struct.Runtime.html)
- An asynchronous Runtime.
- [Runtime](https://docs.rs/struct.RuntimeBuilder.html)- Builder
- A Runtime Builder.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_local.html)- local
- Spawns a task on current thread.

# classes in yew - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew/0.23.0/yew/macro.classes.html

`classes!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

This macro provides a convenient way to create [ Classes](https://docs.rs/html/struct.Classes.html).

The macro takes a list of items similar to the [ vec!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/macro.vec.html) macro and returns a

[instance. Each item can be of any type that implements](https://docs.rs/html/struct.Classes.html)

`Classes``Into<Classes>` (See the
implementations on [to learn what types can be used).](https://docs.rs/html/struct.Classes.html)

`Classes`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let conditional_class = Some("my-other-class");
let vec_of_classes = vec![
    "one-bean",
    "two-beans",
    "three-beans",
    "a-very-small-casserole",
];
html! {
    <div class={classes!("my-container-class", conditional_class, vec_of_classes)}>
        // ...
    </div>
};
```

# Classes in yew::html - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew/0.23.0/yew/html/struct.Classes.html

`pub struct Classes { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/yew/html/classes.rs.html#55-59)#### pub fn [with_capacity](https://docs.rs#method.with_capacity)(n: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/yew/html/classes.rs.html#55-59)

#### pub fn [with_capacity](https://docs.rs#method.with_capacity)(n: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> Self

Creates an empty set of classes with capacity for n elements. (Does not allocate if n is zero.)

Adds a class to a set.

If the provided class has already been added, this method will ignore it.

Adds a class to a set.

If the provided class has already been added, this method will ignore it.

This method won’t check if there are multiple classes in the input string.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This function will not split the string into multiple classes. Please do not use it unless
you are absolutely certain that the string does not contain any whitespace and it is not
empty. Using `push()`  is preferred.

# html_nested in yew - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew/0.23.0/yew/macro.html_nested.html

`html_nested!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

This macro is similar to [ html!](https://docs.rs/macro.html.html), but preserves the component type instead
of wrapping it in

[.](https://docs.rs/html/type.Html.html)

`Html`That macro is useful when, for example, in a typical implementation of a list
component (let’s assume it’s called `List`).
In a typical implementation you might find two component types – `List` and `ListItem`.
Only `ListItem` components are allowed to be children of List`.

You can find an example implementation of this in the [ nested_list](https://github.com/yewstack/yew/tree/master/examples/nested_list) example.
That example shows, how to create static lists with their children.

```
use yew::html::ChildrenRenderer;
use yew::virtual_dom::VChild;
#[derive(Clone, Properties, PartialEq)]
struct ListProps {
    children: ChildrenRenderer<ListItem>,
}
struct List;
impl Component for List {
    type Properties = ListProps;
    // ...
}
#[derive(Clone, PartialEq)]
struct ListItem;
impl Component for ListItem {
    // ...
}
// Required for ChildrenRenderer
impl From<VChild<ListItem>> for ListItem {
    fn from(child: VChild<ListItem>) -> Self {
        Self
    }
}
impl Into<Html> for ListItem {
    fn into(self) -> Html {
        html! { <self /> }
    }
}
// You can use `List` with nested `ListItem` components.
// Using any other kind of element would result in a compile error.
html! {
  <List>
    <ListItem/>
    <ListItem/>
    <ListItem/>
  </List>
}
// In many cases you might want to create the content dynamically.
// To do this, you can use the following code:
html! {
  <List>
    { for some_iter.map(|_| html_nested!{ <ListItem/> }) }
  </List>
}
```
If you used the [ html!](https://docs.rs/macro.html.html) macro instead of

`html_nested!`, the code would
not compile because we explicitly indicated to the compiler that `List`
can only contain elements of type `ListItem` using [, while](https://docs.rs/html/struct.ChildrenRenderer.html)

`ChildrenRenderer<ListItem>`[creates items of type](https://docs.rs/macro.html.html)

`html!`[.](https://docs.rs/html/type.Html.html)

`Html`

---

# props in yew - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew/0.23.0/yew/macro.props.html

`props!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

Build [ Properties](https://docs.rs/html/trait.Properties.html) outside of the

[macro.](https://docs.rs/macro.html.html)

`html!`It’s already possible to create properties like normal Rust structs
but if there are lots of optional props the end result is often needlessly verbose.
This macro allows you to build properties the same way the [ html!](https://docs.rs/macro.html.html) macro does.

The macro doesn’t support special props like `ref` and `key`, they need to be set in the
[ html!](https://docs.rs/macro.html.html) macro.

You can read more about `Properties` in the [Yew Docs](https://yew.rs/concepts/components/properties).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::borrow::Cow;
#[derive(Clone, Properties, PartialEq)]
struct Props {
    #[prop_or_default]
    id: usize,
    name: Cow<'static, str>,
}
struct MyComponent(Props);
impl Component for MyComponent {
    type Properties = Props;
    // ...
}
// You can build props directly ...
let props = yew::props!(Props {
    name: Cow::from("Minka")
});
// ... or build the associated properties of a component
let props = yew::props!(MyComponent::Properties {
    id: 2,
    name: Cow::from("Lemmy")
});
// Use the Rust-like struct update syntax to create a component with the props.
html! {
    <MyComponent key=1 ..props />
}
```

---

#### pub fn [send_stream](https://docs.rs#method.send_stream)<S, M>(&self, stream: S)

This method asynchronously awaits a [ Stream](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.31/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html) that returns a series of messages and sends
them to the linked component.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-3)Panics

If the stream panics, then the promise will not resolve, and will leak.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

This method will not notify the component when the stream has been fully exhausted. If
you want this feature, you can add an EOF message variant for your component and use
[ StreamExt::chain](https://docs.rs/futures-util/0.3.31/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_util/stream/stream/trait.StreamExt.html#method.chain) and

[to chain an EOF message to the original stream. If your stream is produced by another crate, you can use](https://docs.rs/futures-util/0.3.31/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_util/stream/once/fn.once.html)

`stream::once`[to transform the stream’s item type to the component message type.](https://docs.rs/futures-util/0.3.31/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_util/stream/stream/trait.StreamExt.html#method.map)

# yew - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew/latest/yew/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#yew-framework---api-documentation)Yew Framework - API Documentation

Yew is a modern Rust framework for creating multi-threaded front-end web apps using WebAssembly

- Features a macro for declaring interactive HTML with Rust expressions. Developers who have experience using JSX in React should feel quite at home when using Yew.
- Achieves high performance by minimizing DOM API calls for each page render and by making it easy to offload processing to background web workers.
- Supports JavaScript interoperability, allowing developers to leverage NPM packages and integrate with existing JavaScript applications.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-targets-client-side-rendering)Supported Targets (Client-Side Rendering)

- `wasm32-unknown-unknown`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Server-Side Rendering should work on all targets when feature `ssr` is enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-features)Supported Features:

- `csr`: Enables Client-side Rendering support and- `Renderer`
- `ssr`: Enables Server-side Rendering support and- `ServerRenderer`
- `hydration`: Enables Hydration support.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yew::prelude::*;
enum Msg {
    AddOne,
}
struct App {
    value: i64,
}
impl Component for App {
    type Message = Msg;
    type Properties = ();
    fn create(ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Self {
        Self { value: 0 }
    }
    fn update(&mut self, _ctx: &Context<Self>, msg: Self::Message) -> bool {
        match msg {
            Msg::AddOne => {
                self.value += 1;
                true
            }
        }
    }
    fn view(&self, ctx: &Context<Self>) -> Html {
        html! {
            <div>
                <button onclick={ctx.link().callback(|_| Msg::AddOne)}>{ "+1" }</button>
                <p>{ self.value }</p>
            </div>
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    yew::Renderer::<App>::new().render();
}
```

# base64ct 1.8.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/base64ct/^1.6.0

[RustCrypto](https://github.com/rustcrypto): Constant-Time Base64

Pure Rust implementation of Base64 ([RFC 4648](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4648)).

Implements multiple Base64 alphabets without data-dependent branches or lookup tables, thereby providing portable "best effort" constant-time operation.

Supports `no_std` environments and avoids heap allocations in the core API
(but also provides optional `alloc` support for convenience).

## About

This crate implements several Base64 alphabets in constant-time for sidechannel
resistance, aimed at purposes like encoding/decoding the "PEM" format used to
store things like cryptographic private keys (i.e. in the [ pem-rfc7468](https://github.com/RustCrypto/formats/tree/master/pem-rfc7468) crate).

The paper [Util::Lookup: Exploiting key decoding in cryptographic libraries](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.04600.pdf)
demonstrates how the leakage from non-constant-time Base64 parsers can be used
to practically extract RSA private keys from SGX enclaves.

The padded variants require (`=`) padding. Unpadded variants expressly
reject such padding.

Whitespace is expressly disallowed, with the exception of the
[ Decoder::new_wrapped](https://docs.rs/base64ct/latest/base64ct/struct.Decoder.html#method.new_wrapped) and

[modes which provide fixed-width line wrapping.](https://docs.rs/base64ct/latest/base64ct/struct.Encoder.html#method.new_wrapped)

`Encoder::new_wrapped`## Supported Base64 variants

- Standard Base64: `[A-Z]`,`[a-z]`,`[0-9]`,`+`,`/`
- URL-safe Base64: `[A-Z]`,`[a-z]`,`[0-9]`,`-`,`_`
- bcrypt Base64: `.`,`/`,`[A-Z]`,`[a-z]`,`[0-9]`
- `crypt(3)`Base64:- `.`,- `-`,- `[0-9]`,- `[A-Z]`,- `[a-z]`
- PBKDF2 Base64: `[A-Z]`,`[a-z]`,`[0-9]`,`.`,`/`

## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV) Policy

MSRV increases are not considered breaking changes and can happen in patch releases.

The crate MSRV accounts for all supported targets and crate feature combinations, excluding explicitly unstable features.

at your option.

# bincode 2.0.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bincode/^2.0.0-rc.3

# Bincode

A compact encoder / decoder pair that uses a binary zero-fluff encoding scheme. The size of the encoded object will be the same or smaller than the size that the object takes up in memory in a running Rust program.

In addition to exposing two simple functions
(one that encodes to `Vec<u8>`, and one that decodes from `&[u8]`),
binary-encode exposes a Reader/Writer API that makes it work
perfectly with other stream-based APIs such as Rust files, network streams,
and the [flate2-rs](https://github.com/rust-lang/flate2-rs) compression
library.

## Bincode in the Wild

- [google/tarpc](https://github.com/google/tarpc): Bincode is used to serialize and deserialize networked RPC messages.
- [servo/webrender](https://github.com/servo/webrender): Bincode records WebRender API calls for record/replay-style graphics debugging.
- [servo/ipc-channel](https://github.com/servo/ipc-channel): IPC-Channel uses Bincode to send structs between processes using a channel-like API.
- [ajeetdsouza/zoxide](https://github.com/ajeetdsouza/zoxide): zoxide uses Bincode to store a database of directories and their access frequencies on disk.

## Example

```
use ;
;
```
## Specification

Bincode's format is specified in [docs/spec.md](https://github.com/bincode-org/bincode/blob/trunk/docs/spec.md).

## FAQ

### Is Bincode suitable for storage?

The encoding format is stable, provided the same configuration is used. This should ensure that later versions can still read data produced by a previous versions of the library if no major version change has occurred.

Bincode 1 and 2 are completely compatible if the same configuration is used.

Bincode is invariant over byte-order, making an exchange between different architectures possible. It is also rather space efficient, as it stores no metadata like struct field names in the output format and writes long streams of binary data without needing any potentially size-increasing encoding.

As a result, Bincode is suitable for storing data. Be aware that it does not implement any sort of data versioning scheme or file headers, as these features are outside the scope of this crate.

### Is Bincode suitable for untrusted inputs?

Bincode attempts to protect against hostile data. There is a maximum size
configuration available (`Configuration::with_limit`), but not enabled in the
default configuration. Enabling it causes pre-allocation size to be limited to
prevent against memory exhaustion attacks.

Deserializing any incoming data will not cause undefined behavior or memory issues, assuming that the deserialization code for the struct is safe itself.

Bincode can be used for untrusted inputs in the sense that it will not create a security issues in your application, provided the configuration is changed to enable a maximum size limit. Malicious inputs will fail upon deserialization.

### What is Bincode's MSRV (minimum supported Rust version)?

Bincode 2.0 has an MSRV of 1.85.0. Any changes to the MSRV are considered a breaking change for semver purposes, except when certain features are enabled. Features affecting MSRV are documented in the crate root.

### Why does bincode not respect `#[repr(u8)]`?

Bincode will encode enum variants as a `u32`. If you're worried about storage size, we can recommend enabling `Configuration::with_variable_int_encoding()`. This option is enabled by default with the `standard` configuration. In this case enum variants will almost always be encoded as a `u8`.

Currently we have not found a compelling case to respect `#[repr(...)]`. You're most likely trying to interop with a format that is similar-but-not-quite-bincode. We only support our own protocol ([spec](https://github.com/bincode-org/bincode/blob/trunk/docs/spec.md)).

If you really want to use bincode to encode/decode a different protocol, consider implementing `Encode` and `Decode` yourself. `bincode-derive` will output the generated implementation in `target/generated/bincode/<name>_Encode.rs` and `target/generated/bincode/<name>_Decode.rs` which should get you started.

# console_error_panic_hook 0.1.7 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/console_error_panic_hook/^0.1

`console_error_panic_hook`

This crate lets you debug panics on `wasm32-unknown-unknown` by providing a
panic hook that forwards panic messages to
[ console.error](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Console/error).

When an error is reported with `console.error`, browser devtools and node.js
will typically capture a stack trace and display it with the logged error
message.

Without `console_error_panic_hook` you just get something like *RuntimeError: Unreachable executed*

Browser:

Node:

With this panic hook installed you will see the panic message

Browser:

Node:

### Usage

There are two ways to install this panic hook.

First, you can set the hook yourself by calling `std::panic::set_hook` in
some initialization function:

```
extern crate console_error_panic_hook;
use panic;
```
Alternatively, use `set_once` on some common code path to ensure that
`set_hook` is called, but only the one time. Under the hood, this uses
`std::sync::Once`.

```
extern crate console_error_panic_hook;
;
```
### Error.stackTraceLimit

Many browsers only capture the top 10 frames of a stack trace. In rust programs this is less likely to be enough. To see more frames, you can set the non-standard value `Error.stackTraceLimit`. For more information see the [MDN Web Docs](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Microsoft_Extensions/Error.stackTraceLimit) or [v8 docs](https://v8.dev/docs/stack-trace-api).
